question: In the classic 1979 study where mixed evidence drove death-penalty views apart, how was the widening measured?
answer: By asking people how far their views had shifted. Supporters and opponents read the same two studies, rated the one agreeing with them as better, and reported moving further apart. Later studies that measured attitudes directly, before and after, mostly found no widening. The biased rating held up; the polarisation lived largely in the self-report.
move: When people say they changed, check whether anyone measured the before.
ask: Where did I last say I changed my mind without ever recording what I believed before?
source: Miller et al., J Personality Social Psychology, 1993
reference: Miller, McHoskey, Bane & Dowd, The attitude polarization phenomenon: role of response measure, attitude extremity, and behavioral consequences of reported attitude change, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1993
